items.question: Why is neither injunction nor prohibition directly applicable in the case of Shiva?
premises: In this context, injunction is not directly enjoined because it is not suitable for Shiva.
There is also no prohibition of that, because prohibition would refute that principle.
Shiva as the principle cannot be properly limited by direct ritual prescription or negation.
items.inference: Therefore, direct injunction and direct prohibition do not apply to Shiva without undermining the principle itself.
uncertainties: The exact referent of 'in this' (asmin) depends on the immediately preceding ritual or doctrinal context.
items.plain_english: In this case nothing is directly enjoined, because such an injunction does not truly fit Shiva. Nor is there a direct prohibition, since prohibiting it would amount to denying that very principle.

items.question: Where do injunction and prohibition belong in relation to the universal Lord's own nature?
premises: The universal Lord's own form is not subject to real division by injunction and prohibition.
Injunction and prohibition are imagined constructs, whether applied to his own form or to his power.
They do not operate by breaking or negating the Lord's intrinsic nature.
items.inference: Thus injunction and prohibition are conceptual impositions, not realities that divide the Lord's essence.
uncertainties: The phrase 'na svarūpasya khaṇḍane' can be read as limiting the scope of injunction/prohibition rather than denying their conventional use.
items.plain_english: For the Lord, who is the universal Self, injunction and prohibition are only imagined, whether in relation to his own form or to his power. They do not actually break or negate his true nature.

items.question: How should a means be chosen when entering the supreme reality?
premises: In the approach to the supreme reality, suitability depends on what is near or effective for the practitioner.
When a person recognizes a particular means as near, that means may be accepted.
At another time or in another case, that same kind of means may be abandoned.
items.inference: Therefore, acceptance or abandonment of a means is situational, not fixed by an absolute rule.
uncertainties: The subject of 'vetti' is supplied as 'he' from context; the verse states it elliptically.
items.plain_english: But in entering the supreme reality, whatever means one recognizes as near and fitting should be taken up at that time. At other times, or in other cases, it may just as well be set aside.

items.question: What does the Trika teaching say about constraint and equality across sacred forms?
premises: The revered Trika teaching does not impose rigid constraint here.
It declares equality across all gods.
It also declares equality across plants, creepers, mantras, and letters.
items.inference: Therefore, in this teaching, realization is not bound by rigid hierarchies among sacred forms.
uncertainties: The compound 'ovallīmantravarṇayoḥ' is compressed; the exact intended pairing of its members is slightly ambiguous.
items.plain_english: The revered Trika teaching says there should be no rigid constraint here. It teaches an equality that extends to all the gods, and even to plants, creepers, mantras, and letters.

items.question: Why does the realized person see all comings and goings as pervaded by Shiva?
premises: All arrivals and departures are, in truth, pervaded by Shiva.
The realized person directly sees the Shiva-principle as undivided true being.
Because of this vision, no movement falls outside Shiva's reality.
items.inference: Therefore, for one who sees truly, every coming and going is recognized as Shiva-filled.
uncertainties: The verse compresses 'sa hi' into the tokenization; the causal-emphatic force is clear but the sandhi split is editorial.
items.plain_english: Because all comings and goings are filled with Shiva, such a person sees the Shiva-principle as an undivided, unbroken reality.

items.question: Who truly delights in the supreme nondual worship of Bhairava?
premises: One who attains the undivided true being of the Self is like a bee drawn to the fragrance of the ketaki flower.
Such a person is a discerning connoisseur, not like a fly.
Only someone impelled by the Great Lord delights in the supreme nondual worship of Bhairava.
items.inference: Therefore, delight in supreme nondual Bhairava worship belongs to the rare, divinely impelled connoisseur of undivided reality.
uncertainties: The simile's application spans both clauses; the verse links realization of the Self and delight in Bhairava worship by analogy rather than explicit syntax.
items.plain_english: One who reaches the undivided true being of the Self is like a bee, a true connoisseur drawn to the fragrance of the ketaki flower, not like a fly. Only someone moved by the Great Lord takes delight in the supreme nondual worship of Bhairava.
